items.title: What happens after a brand signs an athlete ?
items.description: Brands and athletes have been partners for decades, with sports personalities becoming some of the most recognisable faces in advertising. From the iconic Pepsi and Sachin Tendulkar campaigns of the 1990s to JSW’s association with Neeraj Chopra and CRED’s memorable work featuring Rahul Dravid, some partnerships have gone beyond campaigns to become part of popular culture. At their most successful, the association becomes so strong that the brand is almost inseparable from the athlete, and vice versa. Virat Kohli may have moved from Nike to Puma and now to one8, but the Nike years will also remain etched in the memory of fans who watched him rise. Behind these seemingly effortless associations, however, sits a far more complicated business equation. An athlete partnership is not simply about putting a famous face next to a logo and waiting for attention to follow. Multiple gears, from the athlete’s image and audience to the brand’s category, objectives, media strategy and the economics of the deal, have to fit together for the partnership to work. The equation becomes even more intriguing when the brand has little to do with sport. While an association with an athlete is intuitive for Nike, Puma or adidas, what does a BFSI, consumer goods or electronics brand gain from one? Is it simply borrowing the athlete’s attention and credibility, or creating a larger cultural space for the brand? And then comes the fundamental question: how does a brand choose one athlete from thousands across multiple disciplines to become its face? Prashanth Rao, Partner, Deloitte India, believes four questions need to be asked before brands begin evaluating individual athletes: the objective of the partnership, the need for an athlete, the role the athlete will play and the target audience fit. “Brands must ascertain whether brand awareness, trust or credibility, sales conversion or a talent and culture play is the primary objective of the partnership. Each type of objective requires a different athlete profile and success metrics,” Rao explains. Rao also points to a growing shift from athletes being simply ambassadors or endorsers towards becoming partners who help shape content or products. Audience fit, meanwhile, cannot be reduced to reach. A regional or niche athlete with a highly engaged following may be more relevant to a brand than a national superstar whose audience does not overlap with its target consumer. Tarique , Vice President - Partnerships & Sales, TCM Sports, starts with a similar question, but puts greater emphasis on the business reason for the association. “Question one is why are we even doing this? What are we actually trying to get out of putting our brand next to someone's name? Is it awareness? Is it credibility we don't currently have? Are we trying to crack a younger audience, or a more affluent one?” he asks. For Tarique, defining that objective makes athlete selection less about fame and more about fit. “Reach matters, sure, nobody's saying ignore it. But reach without the right audience behind it is just noise with a huge price tag,” he adds. For Rahul Talwar , Chief Marketing Officer, Axis Max Life Insurance, the principle played out in the company's partnership with Rohit Sharma. Rather than focusing only on his sporting credentials, the brand assessed attributes including performance orientation, trustworthiness, family values, a progressive mindset, wellness credentials, social impact and his self-made journey. “What made our approach distinctive was that we built the partnership around Rohit's off-field persona rather than his on-field success. While his achievements as a captain and world-class performer brought credibility, it was his image as a trusted family man that aligned most closely with our brand,” Talwar says. Bringing Ritika Sajdeh into the partnership as a co-ambassador further reinforced the idea of life insurance as a family decision centred on trust, protection and shared responsibility. Building the partnership before the deal Once the objective and audience are established, the partnership needs to be built as a structure rather than treated as a signing exercise. Rao recommends a quantitative scorecard covering brand fit, audience overlap, brand safety and controversy risk, content authenticity, existing sponsorship commitments and cost. This can narrow the field to three to five athletes before deeper discussions begin. The initial approach should then establish the athlete's understanding of and belief in the brand, as well as their willingness to participate beyond a one-off appearance. From there, brands need to define how the association will work across advertising, product launches, events, grassroots initiatives and content. The commercial agreement can cover fees, posts, appearances, shoots, event participation, image and likeness rights, archival usage, exclusivity and conduct or termination clauses. With AI-generated likenesses and avatars entering marketing workflows, Rao notes that image and likeness rights are becoming increasingly complex. Tarique argues that the creative conversation should happen before the contract is signed, rather than after. “Before you sign, you should already have a rough shape of the year ahead: campaigns, digital content, product drops, retail activity, on-ground moments, PR, maybe even how they plug into the sport itself,” he says. He describes the ideal progression as “Ambassador → Storyteller → Collaborator → Co-creator.” That requires brands to understand the athlete's personality, beliefs, content strengths and ability to participate across formats before deciding what the partnership should look like. The agreement also needs enough flexibility to accommodate changes in the athlete's career, audience and relevance. A rigid contract built around one campaign can quickly become restrictive when the relationship is expected to run for several years. Established stars or rising athletes? The choice between an established athlete and a rising player brings different trade-offs around cost, credibility, flexibility and risk. Rao points to the immediate credibility and awareness established athletes can provide, alongside higher partnership fees and the possibility of brand clutter created by multiple endorsements. “Established athletes usually offer less flexibility in how the relationship can be shaped. Strongly defined public images, existing commitments and contractual expectations leave little wiggle room for brands,” Rao explains. Rising athletes can offer lower partnership costs and greater willingness to collaborate and co-create, while giving brands the opportunity to build alongside their careers. The uncertainty is their future trajectory, and brands may need to invest more in marketing to generate comparable awareness. Rao sees established athletes as suited to objectives requiring scale, immediate credibility and rapid awareness, while rising athletes can serve as longer-term investments. Brands are also increasingly using cohorts of emerging athletes across different sports to diversify audiences and reduce dependence on the trajectory of a single player. Talwar views the decision through the lens of credibility and audience relevance. In a category such as insurance, where trust is central, established sporting personalities can provide immediate national scale and familiarity. “Established players, like captains and sports stars, bring instant national scale, immediate emotional trust, and heavy credibility. When you're trying to build deep-rooted trust in a serious category like insurance, an established name gives you immediate gravity. The trade-off is higher investment and the risk of clutter because they are naturally tied to multiple brands,” Talwar says. At the same time, he points to regional talent and women's sports as ways of reaching more specific and emerging audiences. Axis Max Life's association with Mumbai Indians across both men's and women's teams, including the inaugural Women's Premier League, alongside regional talent such as Allu Sirish, forms part of this broader portfolio approach. Moving beyond the billboard Signing the athlete is only the beginning. The larger challenge is turning the association into something that works across the consumer journey. Tarique believes the strongest partnerships progress from ambassador to storyteller, collaborator and eventually co-creator. He points to Under Armour's association with Neeraj Chopra and Nike's relationship with Serena Williams as examples where the athlete's involvement has extended beyond conventional advertising into content, product and design. The broader principle is to use the athlete's experience and expertise as part of the brand's storytelling rather than simply putting a recognisable face into a campaign. Talwar takes a similar approach through Axis Max Life's wider activation ecosystem. “If your partnership begins and ends with a billboard or a 30-second TV spot, you've missed the point. Good activation is about full-funnel integration, making the athlete an extension of your brand's philosophy,” he says. The brand's activation has included occasion-based campaigns, social content, BTL material, branch merchandise, point-of-sale displays, agent toolkits and customer onboarding collateral featuring its ambassadors. It has also explored AI-led personalised video content featuring Rohit Sharma for customers and sales agents. The aim is to make the athlete relevant across multiple consumer touchpoints rather than confining the relationship to a campaign launch. From endorsement to long-term relationship The final question is whether a brand can build an enduring relationship rather than simply renew an endorsement contract. Rao recommends beginning with an initial six-to-12-month period and linking renewal to defined performance thresholds. If the partnership demonstrates value, it can then develop into a longer-term association, with the athlete's role evolving into content, product development, storytelling and other forms of collaboration. Tarique believes this is where brands often leave value on the table. “Don't judge the partnership by launch-day noise. Impressions and media value from the announcement are nice, but they're not the scoreboard. The real question is, is this thing actually moving consideration, engagement, trial, enquiries, sales, whatever you originally set out to move?” he says. He also cautions against allowing an auto-renewing contract to replace strategy. As the athlete's career and audience evolve, the partnership needs to evolve with them. “If I had to name the single biggest mistake I see, it's treating the athlete like an asset you bought instead of a relationship you're building. When you sign someone, you're not just renting their reach. You're tying your brand to their personality, their behaviour, everything about how they show up publicly,” Tarique says. Talwar similarly argues that a multi-year partnership needs sustained alignment between the athlete's values, life stage and public persona and the brand's long-term positioning. Measurement, meanwhile, needs to go beyond media value. “The more important questions are: Is the athlete strengthening brand trust? Are they improving consideration? Are consumers increasingly associating the athlete's values with the brand? Is the partnership making the brand more relevant and distinctive within its category?” Talwar asks. Rao's framework similarly looks at share of voice and sentiment over time, attributable sales or lead lift, organic mentions outside contractual requirements and whether consumers begin associating the athlete with the brand without prompting. The shift is therefore from treating an athlete as a media asset to building a relationship that can develop with the brand, the athlete and the audience. Fame may create the initial attention, but the partnership has to give consumers a reason to believe the association belongs there. As Tarique puts it, “So the question I'd leave every marketer with isn't ‘who can we sign?’ It's ‘what can we actually build with this person that people will believe?’” The answer determines whether an athlete partnership remains a campaign association or becomes part of the brand's longer-term identity.

items.title: Ryan Roslansky Leaving Microsoft: Leadership Lessons | Vizaca
items.description: Former LinkedIn CEO Ryan Roslansky will leave Microsoft at the end of 2026 rather than relocate to Redmond. Here are the leadership lessons for founders.
